title: Washington v. Roggenkamp
facts: Petitioner Michael Roggenkamp was convicted in the King County Juvenile Court of vehicular homicide and vehicular assault after causing a fatal traffic accident while driving in excess of twice the legal speed limit. The charges were premised upon the trial court's construction of language in the vehicular homicide and vehicular assault statutes (§46.61.522(1) and §46.61.520(1)) regarding operation of a vehicle "in a reckless manner" as meaning "driving in a rash or heedless manner, indifferent to the consequences." Roggenkamp appealed his conviction to the Washington Court of Appeals, asserting that the proper standard to apply in determining whether his conduct fell within the meaning of the statutes was to ask whether it involved "willful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property". The Washington Court of Appeals affirmed Roggenkamp's conviction, leading Roggenkamp to appeal to the Supreme Court of Washington.
questions: What is the appropriate definition under §46.61.522(1) and §46.61.520(1) of the term "in a reckless manner?"
conclusions: Chief Justice Alexander's opinion for the Court concluded that the trial court had been correct in defining "in a reckless manner" as meaning "driving in a rash or heedless manner, indifferent to the consequences." The Court held that the legislative history of the vehicular homicide and vehicular assault statutes indicated an intent to apply a meaning to the term "in a reckless manner" distinct from that of the reckless driving statute, which defines reckless driving as driving with "willful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property."

title: Washington v. Hughes
facts: Petitioner Daniel Hughes was convicted in the Superior Court for Grays Harbor County of first degree theft for cutting down old growth cedar trees. Pursuant to Washington's Sentencing Reform Act of 1981 (§9.94A.535), an enhanced sentence of 90 months imprisonment was imposed rather than the standard 3 to 9 months imprisonment due to the presence of substantial and compelling factors that distinguished the crime from other first degree thefts. Hughes appealed his sentence to the Supreme Court of Washington, claiming that the sentence violated the Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution's right to a trial by jury as the United States Supreme Court's decision in Blakely v. Washington had ruled that the Sixth Amendment requires that any fact other than that of a prior conviction that increases the applicable punishment must be found by a jury beyond a reasonable doubt rather than, as in Hughes' case, by the trial judge.
questions: Do the provisions of the Sentencing Reform Act of 1981 permitting sentencing enhancements violate the Sixth Amendment on their face? If not, did the specific manner in which the sentence was imposed upon Daniel Hughes violate the Sixth Amendment?
conclusions: Justice Fairhurst's opinion for the Court ruled that the Sentencing Reform Act of 1981 was not facially unconstitutional as it could be applied in a manner consistent with the Sixth Amendment. In particular, the Court held that that this would require that establishment of facts used as a basis for an enhanced sentence either be stipulated to by the defendant or that the defendant consent to judicial factfinding. However, the Court declared the particular sentence imposed upon Hughes to be unconstitutional as this was not the case with regard to Hughes' enhanced sentence as it was based upon factual findings of an ongoing pattern of the same criminal conduct that involved determinations and conclusions not limited to merely taking note of prior convictions. Thus, the Court concluded, these factual findings could only be made by a jury.
